title: Belinda
alternative_titles: Belinda. By Maria Edgeworth. In Three Volumes
description: The novel of manners which its author's reputation has most consistently rested upon her, and the plainest proof that the Irish tale-writer of Castle Rackrent was also a searchingly English comic novelist. Belinda Portman, a young woman of good family and no fortune, comes to London under the protection of her early friend Lady Anne Manwarring and is drawn at once into two societies: the elegant and intellectually vain circle of the widow Lady Delacour, and the newer, merrier and more assertive household formed by her friend's husband's marrying relation. The book follows the negotiation of Belinda's marriage - between the suit of a serious foreign banker who wants a wife of domestic habits and the importunities of a fashionable foreign lover - with a steadiness of irony which keeps the heroine's thoughts in view while allowing the reader to see further than she does.
plot_or_argument: Belinda, generous and uninstructed, accepts the protection of Lady Anne and passes under the care of Lady Delacour, a brilliant, unquiet widow whose household is governed by her friendship with a pretender to literary eminences, and whose son is left to the devices of a projecting educator. The domestic peace of the Manwarrings is destroyed by the arrival of a young wife of the new fashion, who brings with her an attached child from the West Indies, a Black girl whose grateful affection for the children of the house she has served supplies one of the most quietly moving episodes in the book. Against this society Belinda's constancy, and the plain good sense which her friends call want of genius, are tested by the perseverance of an admirer of foreign manners and by the jealousy and mismanagement of those who profess to guide her. Her friend Lady Anne is driven into apparent delinquency by a jealous and tyrannical husband, and the novel's most discussed sequence follows the attempts of Belinda and Lady Delacour to relieve her from the confinement into which his authority over her person and her fortune had cast her. The argument, carried by example rather than assertion, is that a woman's independence is a question of law, money and reputation, not of sentiment; that the fashionable reformers of education and of society are charlatans of a mild kind; and that marriage, fairly looked at, is an estate question as much as a matter of the heart.
narrative_structure: A single continuous third-person narrative in short chapters, with the letter and the printed extract introduced where they serve the argument; the action is compressed into a London season and its country excursion, and the plot turns upon two paired crises in the situations of Belinda and of her friend.
principal_characters: Belinda Portman; Lady Anne Manwarring; Mr Manwarring; the fashionable young mistress of the house; Lady Delacour; her son; the attached West Indian child; the serious foreign admirer; the foreign lover of fashion
literary_form: novel of manners and of marriage negotiation in the third person; conversational and didactic comedy
meter_and_prosody: Prose. The style is the plain, quick, unornamented manner its author described as the natural language of a mind in motion: short declarative sentences, the reported exclamation, the abrupt moral aside, and a command of dialogue which carries argument and character at the same moment; the effect is of irony delivered by silence rather than by comment.
historical_context: Published in London in 1801 in three volumes, after Castle Rackrent (1800) had been issued anonymously, and at the moment when the Anglo-Irish Ascendancy, its.absentees and its schemes of education and improvement were the subject of daily argument; the book's quarrel with projectors, with the literary lady and with the fashionable wife belongs to the controversy over female conduct and education carried on by its author's family, and its West Indian child and its planter marriages bring the question of slavery and of the colonial estate into the drawing-room novel.
literary_significance: It is the book by which Maria Edgeworth takes her place in the history of the novel of manners between Fanny Burney and Jane Austen, and it has been the most continuously re-edited and most critically discussed of her fictions, both for its handling of the marriage market and the condition of women and for its treatment of the West Indian child, of affectionate service, and of marriage between the planter and the lady of colour. Its plain style and its refusal of the sentimental crisis were read by later novelists as a lesson in the possible seriousness of comedy, and its last chapter, which leaves its heroine's happiness uncompleted, has long been a test case for the interpretation of her art.
attribution_notes: There has been no dispute as to its authorship: the title page names Maria Edgeworth, whose initials and family position were already known to the book's public from Practical Education and Castle Rackrent, and the novel's composition and publication are documented in the family correspondence which she herself edited.
bibliographical_notes: First published in three volumes at London by J. Johnson in 1801, the year's most noticed novel by a writer already famous in Ireland; it was reprinted in the collected 'Popular Tales' and in later English and American issues, and is now edited from the first edition in the Cambridge and Pickering and Chatto editions of her works.
